title: Why Doesn't Your Stomach Digest Itself?
short_title: Why Doesn't Your Stomach Digest Itself?
description_short:
Why doesn't your stomach digest itself? Mucus is only part of the answer. Surface cells release bicarbonate into the mucus gel, which neutralizes acid close to the stomach wall and keeps the cell surface much less acidic than the contents above. The gel also slows acid down, and other defenses help too, including tightly joined cells and surface repair.

The historical example: in 1822, Alexis St. Martin survived an accidental gunshot wound that left an opening (a fistula) into his stomach. Army surgeon William Beaumont later studied digestion through it, for example with food tied to a string. The experiments were real but ethically troubling, and they revealed digestion, not the modern explanation of the mucus-bicarbonate barrier.

Simplified and historical illustrations: not real medical images and not a portrait. The acid (+) and bicarbonate (−) symbols are a teaching convention.
